Fixed in `28624588f`.

Recipe paths receive an all-platform regular-file preflight, then Unix opens use `O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW`, followed by the authoritative descriptor metadata and size checks. This prevents FIFO blocking and final-component symlink swaps while retaining the once-canonicalized source/base handoff. The legacy scheduler copy path uses the same opener.

The Unix regression uses a watchdog so a future blocking regression fails rather than hanging the suite, and a companion test verifies canonical symlinks to regular recipes remain accepted.

Verification: `cargo test -p goose --test schedule_tool_security` (6 passed) and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

Fixed in `d928905c5`.

The scheduler now opens internal recipe copies without truncation, applies owner-only `0600` permissions on Unix (including pre-existing destinations), and only then truncates and writes the validated bytes. A regression pre-creates a `0644` destination and verifies both the final bytes and mode.

Verification: `cargo test -p goose validated_recipe_copy_makes_existing_destination_owner_private` and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`.

Fixed in 225558c60. Replaced `AllowOrigin::list` with `AllowOrigin::predicate` backed by `is_allowed_origin`, which accepts any port on http://localhost and http://127.0.0.1 while preserving the tauri scheme origins. Added 3 unit tests for the matcher.

**Fixed in cbf6f7f2d49.** When no `.well-known` manifest exists, the fallback now honors a `src` hint from `_mcp.{host}`, validated to be HTTPS and host equal-or-subdomain of the discovery host (so an unauthenticated DNS answer can't redirect elsewhere). Probe order is caller-path -> validated DNS src -> default `/mcp`. See `fallback_honors_validated_dns_src` / `fallback_ignores_cross_host_dns_src`.

Addressed in the latest commit. Moved the dedup into `categorize_tool_requests` so it runs on the provider's tool requests in their original order, before they're split into frontend/backend buckets. The first occurrence now always wins regardless of which bucket each duplicate lands in, and duplicates are also stripped from the filtered history message so duplicate tool_results never enter the conversation.

discussion_comments.comment_body:
One more thing worth raising before merge — separate from the cleanup commit, this is about behavior.

**The `INVALID_REQUEST` error code here may cause the model to retry the denied tool call.**

Semantically, `INVALID_REQUEST` means "your request was malformed" — the natural response from a well-behaved model is to *correct* and retry. That's the opposite of what we want for a policy denial. A model that just got told "you can't run `rm -rf /`" should accept the denial, not infer "I phrased the request wrong, let me try again."

It's worse than just "wrong error code semantics." The message we hand back includes the literal string `"Tool call blocked by plugin"`, which a sufficiently clever model might read as an invitation to *work around* the plugin — rename the tool call, split the command into pieces, try a different tool that does the same thing. We'd be teaching the model that policy denials are obstacles to route around, not boundaries to respect.

Two ways out:

1. **Return a successful `ToolCallResult` with `is_error: true`** instead of an MCP `Err`. The denial then surfaces to the model as a tool *result* ("I called the tool, it told me no"), which is its actual mental model — and tool-result errors don't trigger the retry path that MCP request errors do. Message could be along the lines of *"This tool call was blocked by plugin `<name>`: <reason>. Do not retry; this is a policy denial, not a transient failure."*

2. **At minimum, pick a less retry-friendly MCP error code.** I don't think MCP has a perfect one, but `INTERNAL_ERROR` is less misleading than `INVALID_REQUEST` — it doesn't suggest "fix your request and try again."

I'd lean strongly toward (1) — it's the more honest representation of what happened and removes the retry ambiguity entirely. Either way, I'd want a test that confirms a denied call doesn't trigger a retry storm, since that's the actual user-facing failure mode we're trying to prevent.

(Related, and probably a follow-up PR rather than this one: the deny protocol today only applies to `PreToolUse`. The more useful policy primitives — `BeforeShellExecution` with command-string matchers, `BeforeReadFile` with path matchers — are still fire-and-forget. A plugin author can scope a deny rule to `developer__shell` but not to `rm -rf *`. Worth noting in the PR description so we don't accidentally ship the impression that command-content denial works.)
